summary.text: Hockey-stick and Vandermonde identities rewrite the two sums as \(S_1=\binom{3p}{p}=3W\) and \(S_2=\binom{3p}{p}(1+2p^2R)\), where \(W=\prod_{k=1}^{p-1}(1+2p/k)\); product expansions, alternating-binomial identities, reciprocal reflection, and power-sum congruences then give \(W\equiv1-3p^2H_2\pmod{p^5}\), \(R\equiv\tfrac72H_2\pmod{p^3}\), and \(H_2\equiv0\pmod p\). Setting \(u=W-1\) and \(v=2p^2RW\), the linear term \(7u+3v\) in \((1+u)^4(1+u+v)^3-1\) cancels modulo \(p^5\), while every nonlinear term is already divisible by \(p^6\); the primes \(3\) and \(5\) are handled by direct finite calculation.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 S_1(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{2n}\binom{n+k-1}{k},\qquad
 S_2(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{2n}\binom{n+k-1}{k}^{2},
\]
so that
\[
 a(n)=S_1(n)^4S_2(n)^3.
\]
We prove that, for every prime \(p\geq 3\),
\[
 a(p)\equiv a(1)\pmod {p^5}.
\]
Since \(S_1(1)=S_2(1)=3\), we have
\[
 a(1)=3^7=2187.
\]

Throughout the main part of the proof, \(p\geq7\) is prime. Congruences between rational numbers whose denominators are prime to \(p\) are interpreted in the localized ring \(\mathbb Z_{(p)}\): thus \(x\equiv y\pmod {p^r}\) means that \(x-y\in p^r\mathbb Z_{(p)}\). All harmonic sums occurring below have denominators composed of integers in \(\{1,\ldots,p-1\}\), and hence belong to \(\mathbb Z_{(p)}\). We freely use the elementary rules that such congruences may be added and multiplied, and that multiplication or division by a \(p\)-adic unit does not change divisibility by a power of \(p\).

## 1. Harmonic-sum notation and identities

For \(n\geq0\), put
\[
 H_r(n)=\sum_{j=1}^n\frac1{j^r}\qquad(r=1,2,3,4).
\]
We also need the following strict multiple harmonic sums:
\[
\begin{aligned}
 E_2(n)&=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq n}\frac1{ij},&
 E_3(n)&=\sum_{1\leq i<j<k\leq n}\frac1{ijk},\\
 E_4(n)&=\sum_{1\leq i<j<k<\ell\leq n}\frac1{ijk\ell},
\end{aligned}
\]
and, with the digits denoting the exponents in order,
\[
 H_{rs}(n)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq n}\frac1{i^rj^s},
\qquad
 H_{rst}(n)=\sum_{1\leq i<j<k\leq n}\frac1{i^rj^sj^0k^t};
\]
in the last display the harmless \(j^0\) is only typographical, and the intended definition is
\[
 H_{rst}(n)=\sum_{1\le i<j<k\le n}\frac1{i^rj^sk^t}.
\]
In particular we use \(H_{12},H_{13},H_{21},H_{22},H_{31}\) and \(H_{112},H_{121},H_{211}\).

Splitting products of sums according as their indices are less than, equal to, or greater than one another gives the stuffle identities
\[
\begin{aligned}
 H_1^2&=2E_2+H_2,\
 6E_3&=H_1^3-3H_1H_2+2H_3,\
 24E_4&=H_1^4-6H_1^2H_2+3H_2^2+8H_1H_3-6H_4,\
 H_1H_2&=H_{12}+H_{21}+H_3,\
 H_2^2&=2H_{22}+H_4,\
 H_1H_3&=H_{13}+H_{31}+H_4,\
 H_1E_2&=3E_3+H_{21}+H_{12},\
 H_2E_2&=H_{211}+H_{121}+H_{112}+H_{31}+H_{13}.
\end{aligned} \tag{1}
\]
Here and below, when no argument is shown in an identity, every sum has the same argument \(n\). These formulas can also be proved simultaneously by induction on \(n\): on adjoining the term \(n+1\), use, for example,
\[
 E_2(n+1)=E_2(n)+\frac{H_1(n)}{n+1},\quad
 E_3(n+1)=E_3(n)+\frac{E_2(n)}{n+1},
\]
and the analogous recurrences for the other multiple sums.

We shall also use the following inclusive-prefix identities, obtained directly by writing \(H_r(k)=H_r(k-1)+k^{-r}\) and summing:
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \sum_{k=1}^n\frac{H_1(k)}k&=E_2+H_2,\\
 \sum_{k=1}^n\frac{H_1(k)}{k^2}&=H_{12}+H_3,\\
 \sum_{k=1}^n\frac{H_1(k)}{k^3}&=H_{13}+H_4,\\
 \sum_{k=1}^n\frac{E_2(k)}{k^2}&=H_{112}+H_{13},\\
 \sum_{k=1}^n\frac{H_1(k)^2}{k}&=2E_3+H_{21}+2H_{12}+H_3,\\
 \sum_{k=1}^n\frac{E_2(k)H_1(k)}k
 &=3E_4+H_{211}+H_{121}+3H_{112}+H_{22}+H_{13}.
\end{aligned} \tag{2}
\]
For instance, the second identity follows from
\(H_1(k)=H_1(k-1)+1/k\), and the fifth follows after using
\(H_1(k-1)^2=2E_2(k-1)+H_2(k-1)\). Thus (2) involves no unproved summation formula.

## 2. Basic congruences of harmonic sums

We first show
\[
 H_2(p-1)\equiv0\pmod p,
 \qquad H_4(p-1)\equiv0\pmod p. \tag{3}
\]
Inversion permutes the nonzero residue classes modulo \(p\), so for every positive integer \(s\),
\[
 \sum_{k=1}^{p-1}\frac1{k^s}\equiv\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}k^s\pmod p.
\]
For \(s=2,4\), use
\[
 \sum_{k=0}^{p-1}k^2=\frac{p(p-1)(2p-1)}6
\]
and
\[
 \sum_{k=0}^{p-1}k^4=
 \frac{p(p-1)(2p-1)(3p^2-3p-1)}{30}.
\]
For \(p\ge7\), the relevant denominators are units modulo \(p\), and both right sides are divisible by \(p\). This proves (3).

Reflection \(k\mapsto p-k\) gives stronger information. The exact identity
\[
 \frac1k+\frac1{p-k}
 =-\frac p{k^2}-\frac{p^2}{k^3}-\frac{p^3}{k^4}
   +\frac{p^4}{k^4(p-k)}
\]
shows, after summing from \(1\) to \(p-1\), that
\[
 2H_1+pH_2=-p^2H_3-p^3H_4
 +p^4\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}\frac1{k^4(p-k)}. \tag{4}
\]
Similarly, the exact expansion
\[
 \frac1{(p-k)^2}-\frac1{k^2}
 =\frac{2p}{k^3}+\frac{3p^2}{k^4}
 +p^3\frac{4k-3p}{k^4(p-k)^2}
\]
and invariance of the sum under reflection imply
\[
 2H_3+3pH_4\equiv0\pmod {p^2}. \tag{5}
\]
Indeed, before cancelling a factor \(p\), the displayed summed identity is divisible by \(p^3\); all its remainder terms are \(p\)-integral.

By (3) and (5), and because \(2\) is a unit, we get
\[
 H_3\equiv0\pmod {p^2}. \tag{6}
\]
Then (3), (4), and (6) give
\[
 2H_1+pH_2\equiv0\pmod {p^4},
 \qquad H_1\equiv0\pmod {p^2}. \tag{7}
\]
All sums in (3)--(7) have argument \(p-1\).

Combining these with (1), and observing that \(2,6,24\) are units for prime \(p\ge7\), yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
 E_3&\equiv0\pmod {p^2},& E_4&\equiv0\pmod p,\\
 H_{22}&\equiv0\pmod p,& H_{13}+H_{31}&\equiv0\pmod p,\\
 H_{211}+H_{121}+H_{112}&\equiv0\pmod p.
\end{aligned} \tag{8}
\]
For clarity, the first two assertions follow respectively from the formulas for \(6E_3\) and \(24E_4\) in (1). The assertion about \(H_{22}\) follows from \(2H_{22}=H_2^2-H_4\); the fourth from
\(H_{13}+H_{31}=H_1H_3-H_4\); and the last from
\[
H_{211}+H_{121}+H_{112}=H_2E_2-(H_{13}+H_{31}).
\]

## 3. Three alternating-binomial identities

For later use we record
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \sum_{r=1}^n(-1)^{r-1}\binom nr\frac1{r^2}
 &=\sum_{r=1}^n\frac{H_1(r)}r,\\
 \sum_{r=1}^n(-1)^{r-1}\binom nr\frac{H_1(r)}r
 &=H_2(n),\\
 \sum_{r=1}^n(-1)^{r-1}\binom nr\frac1{r^3}
 &=E_3(n)+H_{12}(n)+H_{21}(n)+H_3(n).
\end{aligned} \tag{9}
\]
Here is a derivation. Pascal's identity gives, for any function \(f\),
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n+1}(-1)^{r-1}\binom{n+1}{r}f(r)
=
\sum_{r=1}^{n}(-1)^{r-1}\binom nr f(r)
+
\sum_{r=1}^{n+1}(-1)^{r-1}\binom n{r-1}f(r).
\]
The elementary identity
\[
 \frac{\binom nk}{k+1}=\frac{\binom{n+1}{k+1}}{n+1}
\]
together with \(\sum_k(-1)^k\binom nk=0\) gives successively
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk\frac1{k+1}&=\frac1{n+1},\\
 \sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk\frac1{(k+1)^2}&=\frac{H_1(n+1)}{n+1},\\
 \sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk\frac{H_1(k+1)}{k+1}&=\frac1{(n+1)^2},\\
 \sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk\frac1{(k+1)^3}
 &=\frac{E_2(n+1)+H_2(n+1)}{n+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Substitution in the Pascal recurrence proves the three formulas in (9) by induction; in the cubic case the last identity of (2) needed is
\(\sum_{r=1}^n(E_2(r)+H_2(r))/r=E_3+H_{12}+H_{21}+H_3\).

## 4. Product expansions and two further harmonic congruences

Define
\[
 Q_m=\prod_{j=1}^m\left(1-\frac pj\right),
\qquad
 \Phi_m=\prod_{j=1}^m\left(1-\frac{2p}{j}\right)
                          \left(1-\frac pj\right),

a\qquad
 W_m=\prod_{j=1}^m\left(1+\frac{2p}{j}\right).
\]
(The isolated letter “a” in the preceding display has no mathematical role; the definitions are those of \(Q_m,\Phi_m,W_m\).)
Multiplying one additional factor and using the recurrences of the multiple harmonic sums gives, for \(m\le p-1\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 Q_m&\equiv1-pH_1(m)+p^2E_2(m)\pmod {p^3},\\
 \Phi_m&\equiv1-3pH_1(m)+2p^2H_2(m)+9p^2E_2(m)\pmod {p^3},\\
 W_m&\equiv1+2pH_1(m)+4p^2E_2(m)+8p^3E_3(m)+16p^4E_4(m)
       \pmod {p^5}.
\end{aligned} \tag{10}
\]
For example, after multiplying the proposed formula for \(Q_m\) by
\(1-p/(m+1)\), its discrepancy from the proposed formula for \(Q_{m+1}\) is
\(-p^3E_2(m)/(m+1)\). For \(W_m\), the discrepancy is
\(32p^5E_4(m)/(m+1)\). The calculation for \(\Phi_m\) is the same multiplication, retaining terms through degree two in \(p\); all omitted terms have a factor \(p^3\). Since all prefix sums and all \(1/(m+1)\) are \(p\)-integral, induction proves (10).

Also,
\[
 \binom{p-1}{r}=(-1)^rQ_r. \tag{11}
\]
This follows by writing the binomial coefficient as
\(\prod_{j=1}^r(p-j)/j\).

We now derive the important congruence
\[
 pH_{12}-\frac32H_2-p^2H_{112}-p^2H_{13}\equiv0\pmod {p^3}. \tag{12}
\]
Set \(n=p-1\). By the first identity in (9) and (11),
\[
 -\sum_{r=1}^n\frac{Q_r}{r^2}=E_2+H_2. \tag{13}
\]
On the other hand, the first expansion in (10), divided by \(r^2\) and summed, gives
\[
 \sum_{r=1}^n\frac{Q_r}{r^2}
 \equiv H_2-p(H_{12}+H_3)+p^2(H_{112}+H_{13})\pmod {p^3}, \tag{14}
\]
where (2) was used. Substitute (13) into (14), then use
\(E_2=(H_1^2-H_2)/2\). The resulting expression differs from the left side of (12) only by
\(H_1^2/2-pH_3\), which is divisible by \(p^3\) by (6) and (7). This proves (12).

We also need the individual congruences
\[
 H_{13}\equiv0\pmod p,
 \qquad H_{112}\equiv0\pmod p. \tag{15}
\]
For the first, the third identity in (9), (11), and the first expansion in (10), now only through degree one, give
\[
 \sum_{r=1}^n\frac{Q_r}{r^3}
 =-(E_3+H_{12}+H_{21}+H_3)
\]
and
\[
 \sum_{r=1}^n\frac{Q_r}{r^3}
 \equiv H_3-p(H_{13}+H_4)\pmod {p^2}. \tag{16}
\]
Using \(H_{12}+H_{21}=H_1H_2-H_3\), equation (16), together with (3), (6), (7), and (8), shows that \(pH_{13}\equiv0\pmod {p^2}\), proving the first part of (15).

For the second, use the middle identity in (9). Equations (10) and (11), multiplied by \(H_1(r)/r\) and summed, give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \sum_{r=1}^n\frac{Q_rH_1(r)}r&=-H_2,\\
 \sum_{r=1}^n\frac{Q_rH_1(r)}r
 &\equiv(E_2+H_2)
 -p(2E_3+H_{21}+2H_{12}+H_3)\\
 &\quad+p^2(3E_4+H_{211}+H_{121}+3H_{112}+H_{22}+H_{13})
 \pmod {p^3}.
\end{aligned} \tag{17}
\]
The identities (1), (8), and (12), applied to (17), first imply
\[
 3E_4+H_{211}+H_{121}+2H_{112}+H_{22}\equiv0\pmod p.
\]
Indeed, subtract (12), use \(H_1^2=2E_2+H_2\) and
\(H_1H_2=H_{12}+H_{21}+H_3\), and note that all remaining terms have the required valuation by (3), (6)--(8). Finally subtract from this congruence the already known congruences
\(E_4\equiv H_{22}\equiv0\) and
\(H_{211}+H_{121}+H_{112}\equiv0\pmod p\). What remains is
\(H_{112}\equiv0\pmod p\), completing (15).

## 5. The two main estimates

Write
\[
 H=H_2(p-1),\qquad W=W_{p-1}.
\]
The third expansion in (10), the identity \(H_1^2=2E_2+H_2\), and (6)--(8) give
\[
 W-1+3p^2H\equiv0\pmod {p^5}. \tag{18}
\]
To see the cancellation explicitly, the left side is congruent modulo \(p^5\) to
\[
 p(2H_1+pH_2)+2p^2H_1^2+8p^3E_3+16p^4E_4.
\]
The four terms are divisible by \(p^5\) by (7), (7), (8), and (8), respectively. Notice also that
\[
 W=\prod_{j=1}^{p-1}\left(1+\frac{2p}{j}\right)
 =\binom{3p-1}{p-1}. \tag{19}
\]

Define
\[
 R=\sum_{k=0}^{p-2}
 \frac{\binom{2p-1}{k}\binom{p-1}{k+1}}
 {(k+1)(p+k+1)}.
\]
We claim
\[
 R-\frac72H\equiv0\pmod {p^3}. \tag{20}
\]
For completeness, we derive the termwise expansion that proves this. From (11), applied with \(p\) and \(2p\),
\[
 \binom{2p-1}{k}\binom{p-1}{k+1}
 =-\Phi_k\left(1-\frac p{k+1}\right).
\]
If \(x=k+1\), then the exact rational expansion
\[
 \frac{1-p/x}{x(p+x)}
 \equiv \frac1{x^2}\left(1-\frac{2p}{x}+\frac{2p^2}{x^2}\right)
 \pmod {p^3}
\]
has remainder \(-2p^3/(x^4(p+x))\). Both \(x\) and \(p+x\) are prime to \(p\), so the remainder is legitimate in \(\mathbb Z_{(p)}\). Multiplying by the second expansion in (10) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \Phi_k\frac{1-p/x}{x(p+x)}\equiv{}&
 \frac1{x^2}-3p\frac{H_1(k)}{x^2}
 +2p^2\frac{H_2(k)}{x^2}+9p^2\frac{E_2(k)}{x^2}\\
 &-\frac{2p}{x^3}+6p^2\frac{H_1(k)}{x^3}
 +\frac{2p^2}{x^4}\pmod {p^3}.
\end{aligned} \tag{21}
\]
Summing (21) for \(k=0,\ldots,p-2\), and remembering the preceding minus sign, gives
\[
 R+\mathcal E\equiv0\pmod {p^3}, \tag{22}
\]
where
\[
 \mathcal E=H_2-3pH_{12}+2p^2H_{22}+9p^2H_{112}
             -2pH_3+6p^2H_{13}+2p^2H_4.
\]
Now (12) and (15) show
\[
 \mathcal E+\frac72H_2\equiv0\pmod {p^3}.
\]
More explicitly,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathcal E+\frac72H_2={}&-3\left(pH_{12}-\frac32H_2-p^2H_{112}-p^2H_{13}\right)\\
 &+p^2(6H_{112}+3H_{13}+2H_{22})-2pH_3+2p^2H_4,
\end{aligned}
\]
and every term on the right is divisible by \(p^3\), by (3), (6), (8), (12), and (15). Subtracting this from (22) proves (20).

## 6. Rewriting the two sums defining \(a(p)\)

The hockey-stick identity gives
\[
 S_1(p)=\sum_{k=0}^{2p}\binom{p+k-1}{k}=\binom{3p}{p}. \tag{23}
\]
Moreover,
\[
 \binom{3p}{p}=3\binom{3p-1}{p-1}=3W. \tag{24}
\]

For the squared sum, Vandermonde's identity gives
\[
 S_2(p)=\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}
 \binom{p-1}{i}\binom{p-1+i}{i}\binom{3p}{p+i}. \tag{25}
\]
Indeed, expand one factor
\(\binom{p-1+k}{p-1}\) by Vandermonde, interchange the \(i,k\) sums, use
\[
 \binom{p-1+k}{k}\binom{k}{i}
 =\binom{p-1+k}{p-1+i}\binom{p-1+i}{i},
\]
and then apply the hockey-stick identity to the remaining sum over \(k\).

The \(i=0\) term of (25) is \(\binom{3p}{p}\). For \(i=k+1\), the elementary factorial identities
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \binom{3p}{p+i}\binom{p-1+i}{i}(p+i)
 &=\binom{3p}{p}\binom{2p}{i}p,\\
 \binom{2p}{k+1}(k+1)&=2p\binom{2p-1}{k}
\end{aligned}
\]
show that the remaining terms equal \(2p^2\binom{3p}{p}\) times the corresponding summands of \(R\). Consequently
\[
 S_2(p)=\binom{3p}{p}(1+2p^2R)=3W(1+2p^2R). \tag{26}
\]

## 7. Final cancellation

Set
\[
 u=W-1,
 \qquad v=2p^2RW.
\]
By (3) and (18), \(u\equiv0\pmod {p^3}\). By (3) and (20), \(R\equiv0\pmod p\), and hence \(v\equiv0\pmod {p^3}\). Equations (23)--(26) give
\[
 a(p)=(3W)^4\bigl(3W(1+2p^2R)\bigr)^3
     =2187(1+u)^4(1+u+v)^3. \tag{27}
\]

The linear part of the last product has an extra cancellation. Namely,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 7u+3v={}&7(W-1+3p^2H)
 +6p^2\left(R-\frac72H\right)+6p^2R\,u. \tag{28}
\end{aligned}
\]
The first term is divisible by \(p^5\) by (18), the second by \(p^5\) by (20), and the third by at least \(p^6\), since \(R\equiv0\pmod p\) and \(u\equiv0\pmod {p^3}\). Thus
\[
 7u+3v\equiv0\pmod {p^5}. \tag{29}
\]
Every nonlinear term in
\((1+u)^4(1+u+v)^3-1-(7u+3v)\) contains at least two factors chosen from \(u,v\), so is divisible by \(p^6\). Equivalently, direct expansion begins
\[
 (1+u)^4(1+u+v)^3-1=7u+3v+u^2P_1(u)+uvP_2(u)+v^2P_3(u,v)
\]
for integer polynomials \(P_1,P_2,P_3\). Hence (29) implies
\[
 (1+u)^4(1+u+v)^3\equiv1\pmod {p^5}.
\]
By (27),
\[
 a(p)\equiv2187=a(1)\pmod {p^5}
\]
for every prime \(p\ge7\).

## 8. The two remaining primes

The only primes with \(3\le p<7\) are \(3\) and \(5\). Direct evaluation of the finite defining sums gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
 p&S_1(p)&S_2(p)\\ \hline
 3&84&1596\\
 5&3003&1933503.
\end{array}
\]
Thus
\[
 a(3)=202402468703748096,
\]
and
\[
 a(3)-2187=3^5\cdot832931969974263.
\]
Likewise,
\[
 a(5)=587835594121137662072707812564687,
\]
and
\[
 a(5)-2187=5^5\cdot188107390118764051863266500020.
\]
So the desired congruence also holds for \(p=3\) and \(p=5\). This completes the proof for every prime \(p\ge3\).
